title: Kolbe before Auschwitz
hook: a friar with a printing press, a magazine for Mary, and a mission to Japan

segments.voice: Yesterday, Faustina and the Divine Mercy. Your line was jesus, I trust in you. Did you find the image and read the line at the bottom? Today, a friar who trusted enough to buy a printing press. Day nine hundred seven.

Ink on his fingers. A Polish Franciscan friar in round glasses bends over an old hand press, cranking out pages of a small magazine. He has very little money and a weak chest, and his own brothers are not sure about this project. The magazine is called the Knight of the Immaculata. He hands copies out, mails them, begs for paper. This path met Maximilian Kolbe at the end of his story, in a starvation cell, offering his life for another prisoner. Today goes back to the middle: the years when he was building something, loudly, with machines.
screen: `INK ON HIS FINGERS.` → `A MAGAZINE CALLED THE KNIGHT.` → `THE MIDDLE OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: The knight came first, in Rome. As a young friar in Rome, Kolbe and a few companions started a movement they called the Militia Immaculatae, the army of the Immaculate, meaning Mary. A knight, in his sense, carried no sword. He carried prayer and a promise to win people over to God through Mary, by any good means at hand. Second, the press. Back in Poland, his means at hand was paper. The magazine grew. He and his brothers built a friary near Warsaw, Niepokalanów, the city of the Immaculate, and filled it with presses and friars who ran them. Kolbe wanted the newest machines. To him, a fast press was a tool for good, the same way a pulpit was. Third, Japan. He sailed east and landed in Nagasaki with almost nothing, not even the language. Soon there was a Japanese edition of the magazine, and a small friary on a hillside outside the city. Fourth, the housetops. Jesus says in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "That which I tell you in the dark, speak ye in the light: and that which you hear in the ear, preach ye upon the housetops." Kolbe treated the newest media of his day as a housetop. The same knight who later stepped forward in Auschwitz spent his working years putting presses, paper and post to that use. Put as a question for today: can this carry something good to someone who needs it?
screen: `THE KNIGHT CARRIES NO SWORD.` · `A CITY OF PRINTING PRESSES.` · `A FRIARY IN NAGASAKI.` · `MEDIA AS A HOUSETOP.` · then, large: `PREACH YE UPON THE HOUSETOPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use media for good. Settle, and breathe. Take out your phone, or just picture its screen. Notice what it usually carries for you: news, noise, arguments, photos, a few kind words. Now let one person come to mind who could use something good today. A friend who's struggling. A parent who's lonely. Decide what you could send them: a photo, a thank-you, a line that helped you. If you pray, you can offer that small message to God before you send it. The bell holds the time.
Militia Immaculatae. The army of the Immaculate, the movement of knights for Mary that Maximilian Kolbe and his companions began in Rome before the printing presses and Nagasaki.
Your line: the knight. Today, before you post or send anything, ask today's question once: does this carry something good to someone? Day nine hundred seven.

howItsDone: Catholics who join the Militia Immaculatae, the movement Kolbe started, consecrate themselves to Mary and pray for others, and Catholic media groups sometimes name Kolbe as an example for their work.
